1268.title: Responsibility
1268.hook: carrying your share, and a bit more
1268.howItsDone: Mussar students work on achrayut by choosing one area where they will be the person who answers, and Jewish teaching often pairs Judah's surety for Benjamin with Rabbi Tarfon's saying in Pirkei Avot.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was kavod, and your line: give honor. Today, a trait with weight on its shoulders.

Famine, and the grain from Egypt is running out. The brothers have to go back down, and the ruler in Egypt has told them: don't come back without your youngest brother. Their father Jacob refuses to let Benjamin go. He has already lost one son. Reuben tries first, with an offer no father could accept. Then Judah steps forward: "I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him." Jacob lets them go. Today's word is what Judah just put on his own back.
screen: `THE GRAIN RUNS OUT.` → `JACOB WON'T LET BENJAMIN GO.` → `I WILL BE SURETY FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: Achrayut. Responsibility. Turn it four ways. First, surety. Judah doesn't say I'll try, or I'll keep an eye on him. He says: require him of my hand. That's the heart of the trait: not doing everything, but being the one who answers for something. Second, the test. In Egypt, a silver cup is found in Benjamin's sack, and the ruler says Benjamin will stay behind as a slave. The others could go home free. Judah steps forward again and asks to stay as a slave in Benjamin's place. His promise gets checked, and it holds. Third, the old question. Much earlier in Genesis, Cain is asked where his brother is, and answers with a question: am I my brother's keeper? God doesn't answer yes or no. He asks back: what hast thou done? Long after, Judah answers Cain's question with his body. Fourth, the share. Pirkei Avot keeps a saying of Rabbi Tarfon: it is not on you to finish the work, and you are not free to walk away from it. Not carrying the whole world, which would crush anyone. Carrying your share, and a bit more, and not setting it down when it gets heavy. Yesterday's honor treated others as weighty. Responsibility lets some of that weight rest on you.
screen: `REQUIRE HIM OF MY HAND.` · `JUDAH OFFERS HIMSELF.` · `AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER?` · `NOT FREE TO WALK AWAY.` · then, large: `CARRY YOUR SHARE.`

segments.voice: Look for something sitting between people, where everyone assumes someone else will handle it: a family call nobody makes, a problem at work that keeps getting forwarded, a promise that was half yours. Pick one and say quietly, the way Judah did, this one is mine, then decide your first step and when: just your share and a bit more. If you pray, you can name it in your prayer.
Achrayut. Responsibility: becoming the one who answers for something, the way Judah answered for Benjamin. Today's word.
Your line: carry your share. You're not asked to finish it, only not to walk away. See you on the next step.

1269.title: Harmful speech
1269.hook: speech that harms, even when it's true
1269.howItsDone: Some Jews study the laws of guarding speech a little each day, and some communities and schools hold days or hours set aside for speaking no lashon hara at all.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was achrayut, and your line: carry your share. Today a new stretch begins, on speech, starting with the tongue.

Did you hear about Dan? He got let go. Apparently he'd been missing deadlines for months. Two people at a coffee machine. Every word is true. Nobody is lying, nobody is shouting, and nobody would call it cruel. It's just news, passed along with a little lift in the voice. Dan isn't there. He'll never know this conversation happened. And yet Jewish tradition has a name for that sentence, and it treats it as a serious wrong.
screen: `EVERY WORD IS TRUE.` → `DAN ISN'T THERE.` → `THE SENTENCE HAS A NAME.`

segments.voice: Lashon hara. Literally, the evil tongue: speech that harms, even when it's true. You got a first glimpse of it long ago, with tzara'at, the skin affliction read as speech made visible. Turn it four ways. First, the true part. Saying something false about a person is a different wrong, and it gets its own name later this week. Lashon hara is about true things: a failure, a weakness, an embarrassing story, told in a way that lowers someone. Accurate isn't the same as kind. Second, the story. In Numbers, Miriam and Aaron speak against their brother Moses. God's anger burns, and Miriam is struck with a skin disease and shut outside the camp for seven days, while the whole people waits for her. Deuteronomy later says to remember what God did to Miriam on the way out of Egypt, and tradition reads that as a warning about speech. Third, the three it wounds. The Talmud, in tractate Arakhin, says lashon hara kills three: the one who speaks it, the one who hears it, and the one it's about. The speaker gets smaller. The listener can't unhear it. And the one it's about pays for a conversation they weren't in. Fourth, the exception. Some harmful truth may be spoken when it's needed to protect someone, like warning a friend about a business partner who cheats. The rules are careful, and the purpose has to be help, not entertainment. That's the line: does this sentence protect someone, or just make a good story?
screen: `TRUE, AND STILL HARMFUL.` · `REMEMBER WHAT GOD DID TO MIRIAM.` · `IT KILLS THREE.` · `PROTECTION, NOT ENTERTAINMENT.` · then, large: `NO GOSSIP.`

segments.voice: Picture where gossip usually finds you: a group chat, a lunch table, a family dinner, the moment someone's name comes up and the story starts to lean. Find an easy sentence for that moment, like I don't really know the whole story, or let's talk about something else, and rehearse it once in your head. If you pray, you can ask for help with it in your own words.
Lashon hara. The evil tongue: true words about someone that lower them, when no one needs protecting. Today's word.
Your line: no gossip. A true word can still be a heavy one. Day done.

1270.title: The Chafetz Chaim (Psalm 34:13–14)
1270.hook: Israel Meir Kagan's book on speech takes its name from "Who is the man that desireth life"
1270.howItsDone: Some Jews study a short section of the Chafetz Chaim's laws of speech each day, often in study groups or with a daily calendar, and Psalm 34's verses on the tongue are sung in some prayer services.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was lashon hara, and your line: no gossip. Today, the book that gathered the rules for it.

A peddler is walking through the towns of Galilee, calling out like any street seller: who wants to buy the elixir of life? A rabbi named Yannai, studying nearby, hears him and calls him over. The peddler doesn't open a bottle. He opens a book of Psalms and points to a verse. That's the story the midrash tells. The verse would one day name a book, and the book would name the man who wrote it.
screen: `WHO WANTS THE ELIXIR OF LIFE?` → `HE OPENS THE PSALMS.` → `A VERSE BECOMES A NAME.`

segments.voice: The Chafetz Chaim. In Hebrew, chafetz chaim means desiring life. Turn it four ways. First, the verse. Psalm thirty-four, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, asks: "Who is the man that desireth life, and loveth days, that he may see good therein?" A question with a lot of hands going up. Then the answer: "Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile." Not a diet. Not a medicine. The tongue. Second, the book. A rabbi named Israel Meir Kagan, living among the Jews of Eastern Europe, wrote a book gathering the laws of guarding speech: what counts as lashon hara, when speaking is forbidden, when it's required to protect someone. He named it from this verse: Chafetz Chaim. Third, the man who became his book. People came to call the author by its title, and the name stuck. An unusual kind of fame, being named for a book about what not to say. Fourth, the next verse. The psalm doesn't stop at keeping quiet: depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it. Guarding the tongue isn't only a fence. It makes room for peace. Yesterday named the harm; today hands it a discipline, with a verse at the front. And the question still stands open: who wants life?
screen: `WHO IS THE MAN THAT DESIRETH LIFE?` · `A BOOK OF THE LAWS OF SPEECH.` · `THE MAN BECAME HIS BOOK.` · `SEEK PEACE, AND PURSUE IT.` · then, large: `KEEP THY TONGUE FROM EVIL.`

segments.voice: Touch the tip of your tongue to the back of your teeth and feel how small it is, and how much it does. Run through the day ahead, pick one conversation that could easily tilt, and decide now what you'll do if a story starts: let it pass, or turn it toward something good. If you pray, say the psalm's line, keep thy tongue from evil; if not, hold the question, who wants life?
The Chafetz Chaim. Desiring life: the psalm's question, the title of Israel Meir Kagan's book on guarding speech, and the name people gave the man. Today's word.
Your line: keep thy tongue from evil. The psalm goes on: seek peace, and pursue it. Same time tomorrow.

1271.title: Carrying tales
1271.hook: telling someone what another said about them
1271.howItsDone: Jews who study the laws of speech learn rechilut as its own category alongside lashon hara, and the tradition of editing a report for the sake of peace is often taught from the Talmud's reading of Sarah's laugh.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the Chafetz Chaim, and your line: keep thy tongue from evil. Today, the tale that travels between two people.

In Genesis, Sarah overhears a visitor promise that she will have a son, and she laughs to herself. She's old, she thinks, and her husband is old too. Then God speaks to Abraham about the laugh, and repeats what Sarah said. Listen closely to the repeat. God reports that Sarah wondered whether she, being old, could bear a child. The part about Abraham being old is gone. The Talmud, in tractate Yevamot, noticed the missing words, and it says God left them out for the sake of peace in the home.
screen: `SARAH LAUGHS.` → `GOD REPEATS IT TO ABRAHAM.` → `ONE PART IS MISSING.`

segments.voice: Rechilut. Carrying tales: telling someone what another person said or did about them. Turn it four ways. First, the verse. Leviticus says: "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people." Up and down, from house to house. Second, another peddler. Yesterday's peddler sold life. Rashi connects the word for talebearer with the trader who walks door to door with a pack. As Rashi describes it, the talebearer works a similar route: going into people's houses to find something bad, then telling it in the market. Third, what makes it different. The Chafetz Chaim treats rechilut as its own kind of harmful speech. Lashon hara lowers someone in others' eyes. Rechilut aims at a relationship. So-and-so said this about you. Your sister thinks you're selfish. The words may be accurate, and the carrier may even think they're helping. But two people at peace an hour ago now aren't. Fourth, what God left out, an edit you may remember from early on as peace over precision. The full report was available, and accurate. In the Talmud's reading, God edits it for peace between a husband and wife. No one is asked to invent anything. The question is simpler: when you know what someone said about someone else, do they need to hear it? Or does the story only want a carrier?
screen: `NOT A TALEBEARER AMONG THY PEOPLE.` · `LIKE A PEDDLER, DOOR TO DOOR.` · `IT AIMS AT A RELATIONSHIP.` · `THE PART GOD LEFT OUT.` · then, large: `DON'T CARRY TALES.`

segments.voice: Let one remark come to mind that someone made about someone else, which the second person doesn't know yet: a comment at work, in the family, a screenshot. Picture the two of them still at peace, and ask whether passing it on would protect anyone or only move a hurt from one house to another. If it protects no one, set it down like a peddler putting down a pack; if you pray, you can ask for peace between them.
Rechilut. Carrying tales: going from one person to another with what was said about them, like a peddler with a pack. Today's word.
Your line: don't carry tales. A story with no carrier stops where it is. Go in peace.

1272.title: Slander
1272.hook: spreading falsehood that harms a name
1272.howItsDone: Jewish teaching on speech distinguishes lashon hara, hurtful truth, from motzi shem ra, hurtful falsehood; repentance for it is understood to include repairing the harm, not only stopping.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was rechilut, carrying tales, and your line: don't carry tales. Today, a harm that's heavier because it isn't even true.

Who started it? By the fourth telling, nobody can say. A parent at school pickup sees a for-sale sign on a family's lawn and wonders aloud whether they're in trouble with money. The next parent repeats it as a fact. By Friday the family is losing the house. None of it happened. They're moving to be closer to a grandmother who needs help. But the story has a life of its own, and the true version never travels as fast. Jewish teaching has a separate, heavier name for harmful speech that's false.
screen: `A FOR-SALE SIGN.` → `A GUESS BECOMES A FACT.` → `THE TRUTH TRAVELS SLOWER.`

segments.voice: Motzi shem ra. Word for word, bringing out a bad name. Turn it four ways. First, it's the Torah's own phrase. In Deuteronomy a man turns against his new wife and invents an accusation against her, and the text says he "hath brought up an evil name" on her. The law takes her side. The lie is treated as an injury, and he pays for it. A name, in this picture, can be wounded. Second, where it sits. The Chafetz Chaim, among other teachers, draws a line. Lashon hara is a hurtful thing that's true. Motzi shem ra is a hurtful thing that's false. The first is already forbidden; the second adds a lie to the harm, and tradition counts it heavier. Third, the commandment behind it: "Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour." Some hear that only in a courtroom. The teachers of speech hear it at the kitchen table too, because a rumor is testimony with no judge to check it. Fourth, the small versions. A guess passed along as fact. A detail dropped that would have changed the story. "I heard she..." with nothing behind it. And because a false story keeps moving, Jewish teaching on repentance asks for more than going quiet. It asks for repair: going back, as far as you can reach, and setting it straight. That's harder than silence. It's also the one thing that goes after the story once it has left.
screen: `BRINGING OUT A BAD NAME.` · `TRUE HARM, OR FALSE HARM.` · `NO FALSE WITNESS, EVEN AT HOME.` · `REPAIR, NOT JUST SILENCE.` · then, large: `NO FALSE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Look back for one thing you said or let stand that was wrong about someone, maybe a guess about why a friend canceled, and see whoever heard it from you. Find the plain sentence that would set it straight, I said that, and I was wrong, and say it once, silently. If nothing comes to mind, picture a false story going around and the one true sentence that could replace it; if you pray, you can ask for the nerve to say it out loud.
Motzi shem ra. Bringing out a bad name: harmful speech that is also false. The phrase comes from Deuteronomy itself. Today's word.
Your line: no false names. Repair is harder than silence, and it reaches further. Gently, until tomorrow.

1273.title: Feathers in the wind
1273.hook: a folk tale: gossip is like feathers from a pillow, impossible to gather back
1273.howItsDone: Jewish teachers, parents and schools often tell the feathers tale when teaching about lashon hara, as a picture of why harmful speech can't be fully undone.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was motzi shem ra, bringing out a bad name, and your line: no false names. Today, a tale about how far words go once they leave.

A pillow, a knife, and a windy hill. That's the whole set for a story Jewish teachers tell about speech. Someone in a small town has been spreading talk about a neighbor. The talk turns out to be cruel, and the person, sick about it, goes to the rabbi to ask how to make it right. The rabbi says: take a feather pillow up the hill, cut it open, and come back. Strange, but easy. The person slits the pillow, watches the wind take the feathers, and comes back, ready to be forgiven. Good, says the rabbi. Now go and gather every feather.
screen: `A PILLOW, A KNIFE, A WINDY HILL.` → `CUT IT OPEN.` → `NOW GATHER EVERY FEATHER.`

segments.voice: Feathers in the wind. Turn the tale four ways. First, where it comes from. You won't find it in the Torah or the Talmud. It's a folk tale, and tellers hang it on different rabbis and different towns. It doesn't need a famous source to land: anyone who has opened a pillow knows how feathers behave. Second, the shape of the lesson. Scattering takes a moment. Gathering takes forever, and still fails. Words leave in a breath, land in ears you'll never meet, and get repeated in voices that aren't yours. Third, who the story is about. Not a villain. Someone who is sorry and wants to fix it. The tale doesn't say repentance is useless; yesterday's repair still matters. But even real regret can't recall every feather. Some of the harm is already past reaching. Fourth, so the care belongs before the words. Proverbs puts the stakes bluntly: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue." The tale turns that line into something you can see. And today a pillow opens with one tap. A forwarded message, a screenshot, a post: each a feather with a timestamp, blowing over hills the sender will never climb. The moment of most control is the second before speaking, while every feather is still inside.
screen: `A FOLK TALE, NOT A TALMUD PAGE.` · `EASY TO SCATTER, HARD TO GATHER.` · `EVEN REAL REGRET CAN'T RECALL THEM.` · `DEATH AND LIFE IN THE TONGUE.` · then, large: `YOU CAN'T GATHER FEATHERS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a conversation coming up, a call, a meeting, a group chat, and one sentence already waiting on your tongue: a joke at someone's expense, a complaint about someone absent, news that isn't yours to share. Hold it like a pillow in your hands and ask where it could blow once it's out. Decide now, while it's still sealed, whether it goes out at all; if you pray, you can ask for a guarded mouth.
Feathers in the wind. A folk tale: harmful words, like a pillow's feathers, scatter in a moment and can never all be gathered back. Today's word.
Your line: you can't gather feathers. Every one is still inside until you speak. See you on the hill.

1274.title: Listening counts too
1274.hook: the tradition forbids listening to gossip, not only speaking it
1274.howItsDone: Jewish laws of speech, as the Chafetz Chaim sets them out, treat listening to and believing lashon hara as forbidden alongside speaking it; observant Jews try to change the subject or leave when gossip starts.

segments.voice: Yesterday: feathers in the wind, and your line: you can't gather feathers. Today closes this stretch on speech by turning to the other side of every conversation.

Gossip is a two-person job. One to say it, and one to lean in. Someone lowers their voice: okay, don't repeat this. The listener's face does half the work: eyebrows up, chair pulled closer, tell me everything. Without that face, gossip can die in the first sentence. All week the focus has been on the mouth. Jewish teaching on speech doesn't let the ear off the hook as an innocent bystander.
screen: `GOSSIP NEEDS TWO.` → `THE LISTENER LEANS IN.` → `THE EAR IS NOT A BYSTANDER.`

segments.voice: Listening counts too. Turn it four ways. First, the verse. In Exodus, among the laws for honest courts: "Thou shalt not utter a false report." The rabbis of the Talmud read that line in two directions at once: don't spread a false report, and don't take one in. The verse that guards the mouth guards the ear. Second, the body. The Talmud, in tractate Ketubot, asks a playful question: why are human fingers shaped like pegs? So that if a person hears something unfit, they can put their fingers in their ears. And why is the ear hard but the earlobe soft? So the lobe can be folded in to close it. Half a smile and half serious: the ear can close, and knowing it can is the point. Third, what not listening looks like. It's rarely a speech. Changing the subject. Asking, should we be talking about this? Finding a reason to refill the coffee. And if the words have already landed, the teachers of speech, the Chafetz Chaim among them, ask the listener at least not to believe it, to hold it as unproven rather than true. Fourth, the stretch behind you: responsibility, then lashon hara, the Chafetz Chaim, rechilut, motzi shem ra, feathers that can't be gathered. Each piece closes a door, and the ear closes the last one: gossip with nobody to hear it has nowhere to go.
screen: `DON'T SPREAD IT, DON'T TAKE IT IN.` · `FINGERS SHAPED LIKE PEGS.` · `CHANGE THE SUBJECT, OR DOUBT IT.` · `A WEEK OF GUARDED SPEECH.` · then, large: `DON'T LISTEN.`

segments.voice: Picture a place where talk about other people tends to start, a break room, a family dinner, a group chat that lights up at night, and see the moment it begins: the lowered voice, the did you hear. Choose your exit, a question like is this ours to talk about, a new topic, or just standing up to get water, and play it through once, calmly, until it feels like something you could do. If you pray, you can ask for ears that know when to close.
Listening counts too. In Jewish teaching on speech, hearing gossip and accepting it is part of the harm, not just saying it. Today's word.
Your line: don't listen. What's already heard can be held as unproven. And that's a whole stretch on speech, done.
